blocks.prompt: The Fruit That Kept Sailors Alive
blocks.text: Long ago, sailors were afraid of a sickness called scurvy. On long trips across the sea, they ate the same dried food for months. They had no fresh fruit. Their gums grew sore, their teeth fell out, and some of them died. No one knew why. Then people noticed something. Sailors who ate lemons and other citrus fruit did not get sick. Lemons are full of a thing called vitamin C, and our bodies need it to stay healthy. Ships began to carry barrels of lemons and limes on every long voyage. The sour juice kept the sailors strong. A lemon is more than a sour snack. Its juice is so acidic that it can clean a dirty pot or stop a cut apple from turning brown. If you write on paper with lemon juice and let it dry, the words seem to vanish. Hold the paper near a warm lamp, and the hidden writing turns brown and appears again.

blocks.prompt: The Fruit With No Wild Home
blocks.text: No wild lemon tree has ever been found. That is a strange fact for a fruit sold in almost every store on Earth. Scientists who study plants believe the lemon is a hybrid, a cross between two other citrus fruits: the sour orange and a large, thick-skinned fruit called the citron. Somewhere in Asia, hundreds of years ago, these two fruits crossed and produced the lemon we know today. Because the lemon began as a hybrid, growers cannot simply plant a seed and expect a good tree. Instead, they join a branch from a proven lemon tree onto the root of a hardier plant, a trick called grafting. Every lemon in the store traces back through grafting to a small number of parent trees. A lemon tree is evergreen, which means it never drops all its leaves at once. It can carry buds, white flowers, small green fruit, and ripe yellow lemons all on the same day. One healthy tree may give hundreds of lemons in a single year, and it keeps producing for decades. Lemons do not sweeten after they are picked, unlike bananas or peaches. Whatever sourness a lemon has when it leaves the tree, it keeps. Growers pick lemons while they are still slightly green and let them turn yellow on the way to the store. The bright color we expect is partly a matter of timing, not just ripeness.

blocks.prompt: The Chemistry Set You Can Hold
blocks.text: Bite into a lemon and your whole face reacts. Eyes squeeze shut, cheeks draw in, and saliva floods your mouth. That reaction is not random. It is your body responding to acid. The juice of a lemon is roughly five to six percent citric acid, and on the pH scale, which measures how acidic something is, lemon juice sits near two. Pure water sits at seven, in the middle. The lower the number, the stronger the acid, so a two is very sour indeed. Sourness is one of the five basic tastes, and it evolved as a warning. Unripe fruit is sour and acidic, so the sour taste once told animals to wait until fruit ripened and sweetened. The lemon, oddly, never gets the memo. It stays sour to the end, and humans have learned to prize it for exactly that. That acid does useful work in a kitchen. Squeeze lemon over a cut apple and the browning slows, because the acid blocks the reaction between the fruit and the air. Add lemon juice to milk and it curdles, the first step in making some soft cheeses. Acid also brightens flavor, which is why a cook finishes a rich dish with a squeeze of lemon rather than more salt. Outside the kitchen, the same acid cuts through grease and lifts stains, which is why you find lemon listed on so many cleaning bottles. The strangest trick is electrical. Push a copper coin and a zinc nail into a lemon, connect them with wire, and you have built a simple battery. The acid inside the lemon lets charged particles move between the two different metals, and that flow is an electric current. A single lemon makes only a tiny amount, not enough to light a normal bulb, but link several lemons together and the current grows. The lemon is not storing electricity like a real battery. It is providing the acid bath that lets a chemical reaction between the metals happen. A humble sour fruit turns out to be a small chemistry set you can hold in one hand.

6.title: The Lemon That Saved Sailors

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Ordinary Fruit With an Extraordinary Past
blocks.text: A lemon is such an ordinary object that it takes an act of imagination to see how strange its history is. The fruit has no confirmed wild ancestor. Genetic studies point to the lemon as a hybrid, most likely a cross between the bitter orange and the citron, two citrus fruits that themselves trace back to the forests of South and Southeast Asia. From that region, citrus spread slowly along trade routes, carried by merchants, armies, and monks who valued the fruit as much for its scent and its supposed medicine as for its taste. By the time lemons reached the Mediterranean, they were a luxury. Wealthy Romans grew them for display, and for centuries a lemon on the table was a quiet announcement of money. The lemon's most consequential chapter, though, was written at sea. Long ocean voyages once carried an invisible passenger called scurvy, a disease that loosened teeth, reopened old wounds, and killed sailors by the thousands. For a long time no one understood it. The cause was a lack of vitamin C, which the human body, unlike most animals, cannot manufacture for itself and cannot store for long. In 1747 a naval surgeon named James Lind ran one of the first controlled experiments in medical history. He divided sick sailors into groups and gave each group a different treatment. The men given oranges and lemons recovered; the others did not. It took decades for navies to act on the result, but once they did, citrus rations changed the reach of ships and, with them, the shape of empires. The sour fruit that had been a rich person's ornament became a tool of sea power. Behind the history sits simple chemistry. The sharpness of a lemon comes mainly from citric acid, which makes up around five percent of the juice and pushes its pH down near two, close to the acidity of stomach fluid. That acidity explains most of what a lemon can do. It preserves, because few microbes thrive in strong acid. It cleans, because acid dissolves the mineral deposits and grease that water alone leaves behind. It transforms food, curdling milk into cheese and firming raw fish in a dish like ceviche without any heat. The same molecules that warn the tongue with sourness are the ones that make the fruit useful. The lemon has also become a fixture of language and art. We speak of a broken car as a lemon, of turning sour luck into lemonade, of a person's face puckering as if they had bitten one. Painters of earlier centuries tucked a half-peeled lemon into their still lifes, its bright rind curling down, both to show off their skill and to hint that beauty and bitterness sit side by side. For a fruit with no wild home and no natural sweetness, the lemon has traveled remarkably far. It has crossed oceans, guarded sailors, flavored kitchens, cleaned houses, and lent its name to our disappointments. Not bad for something almost no one eats whole.
